title: Geopolitical fragmentation is reshaping cyber strategy while AI, quantum, supply-chain, and skills readiness lag
source_unit: PwC, 2026 Global Digital Trust Insights: New world, new rules—Cybersecurity in an era of uncertainty
geography: Business and technology executives across 72 countries, spanning private-sector and public-service industries

denominator.unit: business and technology executives across 72 countries in the published survey frame

cyber_investment_priority.unit: percent ranking cyber-risk investment among their top three strategic priorities in response to geopolitical volatility

infrastructure_location.unit: percent ranking changes in critical-infrastructure location among top three cyber-strategy changes

operating_policy_change.unit: percent ranking changes in trade and operating policies among top three responses

geopolitical_channel.value: fractured alliances, trade disputes, weakened institutions, and supply-chain disruption are reshaping cyber vulnerabilities

observations.method: PwC Global Digital Trust Insights 2026 online survey of business and technology executives conducted May-July 2025, summarized across 72 countries.
observations.uncertainty: Executive perceptions and planned strategy changes do not measure realized cyber resilience, actual investment, incident frequency, or population-level digital safety.
observations.subgroup: Business and technology leaders, critical-infrastructure operators, public services, suppliers, workers, customers, and communities exposed to cyber disruption.
observations.counterinterpretation: Strategic reprioritization can strengthen resilience and localization, but it can also increase fragmentation, cost, redundancy, and exclusion from global systems.

denominator.unit: security leaders, chief operating officers, and operations directors answering readiness questions

overall_readiness.unit: percent feeling very capable across all surveyed cyber vulnerabilities

capability_gap.value: roughly half report their organization is at best somewhat capable of withstanding attacks targeting specific vulnerabilities

weak_spots.value: legacy systems and supply-chain vulnerabilities remain among the weakest spots and frequent targets for nation-state actors

observations.method: PwC subgroup analysis of security leaders and operations executives within the Global Digital Trust Insights survey.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived capability is not a penetration test, incident record, or independent audit; subgroup composition and self-assessment can shape the result.
observations.subgroup: Security leaders, operations directors, legacy-system owners, suppliers, critical infrastructure, public agencies, and users dependent on connected services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Self-identified gaps may reflect more mature risk awareness, while organizations reporting confidence may still face unknown or systemic vulnerabilities.

observations.period: 2026; proactive defense, AI, and data governance

denominator.unit: surveyed organizations' cyber spending, AI defense, and data-risk governance frame

proactive_spending.unit: percent spending significantly more on proactive than reactive cybersecurity measures

balanced_spending.unit: percent reporting roughly equal reactive and proactive cybersecurity spending

data_controls.unit: percent reporting full implementation of all surveyed enterprise data-risk measures

ai_defense.value: AI and agentic AI are among the leading priorities for threat hunting, cloud security, data protection, and cyber defense

observations.method: PwC aggregate analysis of cyber spending, data governance, and AI-security priorities.
observations.uncertainty: Budget shares and implementation claims do not establish effectiveness, proportionality, privacy protection, or whether AI tools reduce total cyber risk.
observations.subgroup: Security teams, data stewards, AI developers, employees, customers, regulators, and organizations with different cyber maturity and resources.
observations.counterinterpretation: Reactive spending can be rational during acute incidents, and AI tools may improve detection and response if governance, data quality, and human oversight are strong.

denominator.unit: enterprise quantum-resistant security and cyber-talent readiness frame

quantum_priority.value: quantum computing ranks among the threats organizations are least prepared to address, while fewer than 10 percent prioritize it in budgets

quantum_completion.unit: percent reporting implementation of all leading quantum-resistant measures surveyed

skills_barrier.unit: percent prioritizing AI and machine-learning tools to help close cyber capability gaps

talent_mechanism.value: knowledge and skills gaps remain major barriers to AI-enabled cyber defense and post-quantum readiness

observations.method: PwC aggregate analysis of quantum-readiness, AI-security, and cyber-talent questions.
observations.uncertainty: Readiness percentages are executive reports of organizational status, not technical verification or a forecast of when quantum threats will materialize.
observations.subgroup: Cybersecurity workers, technology leaders, organizations with legacy cryptography, public agencies, critical infrastructure, and education or training systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low current readiness may reflect rational sequencing while standards, threat intelligence, and usable post-quantum tools mature; early preparation can still reduce future switching costs.

related_sources.claim: ITU ICT Development Index 2026 provides complementary global connectivity and digital-infrastructure conditions.
BIS Annual Economic Report 2026 provides complementary financial, geopolitical, and digital-trust system analysis.

boundary: This record adds an executive-perception and organizational-readiness route across geopolitics, cyber risk, critical infrastructure, AI defense, quantum readiness, data governance, and skills. It uses published aggregate survey results and report synthesis, not respondent-level records, technical audits, incident microdata, individual privacy outcomes, or proof that planned investment creates resilience.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official PwC 2026 Global Digital Trust Insights materials were reviewed for the 3,887-executive/72-country frame, geopolitical strategy response, readiness, cyber spending, AI defense, quantum readiness, and skills gaps.
